turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good morning. I'm Dr Shah. Do come in and sit yourselves down. What brings you in today?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Good morning, doctor. Thank you for seeing me. I'm afraid my lower back has been rather troublesome.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's been hobbling about the house. I told him he ought to come and see you.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm sorry you've been dealing with that. Where exactly does it sit, and how does it behave through the day?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): It's across the bottom of my back, doctor, more to the right, and it travels a little into the...
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): Into the leg?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): No, not the leg, doctor. The pain stays in the lower back and the right buttock, and then it stops. It's a dull ache, quite sharp if I bend to lift something.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long has this been going on?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): A few weeks, doctor. About three weeks, I should think.
[SEG0010] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Longer than that. We moved house six weeks ago, and his back went that first weekend, shifting boxes.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, perhaps it did begin with the move. I had thought it was only these last three weeks that it became properly bad.

[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): So the back pain has been somewhere between three and six weeks, and neither of you is quite settled on which. That's fine, we can work with that. Was there a particular twist, or a fall?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): No fall, doctor. I was carrying a chest of drawers down the stairs. I felt something go, but I carried on, which was foolish of me.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any numbness or tingling in the legs, or around the saddle area, the groin and back passage?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): I wouldn't say numb, doctor. There was an evening last week, driving back from the warehouse, when my right foot felt... well...
[SEG0016] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He told me it had gone to sleep.
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, odd, as though it had gone to sleep. It came back once I got out and walked about. There is no persistent numbness, and nothing around the saddle area.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. Your waterworks — any trouble passing urine, any leaking, or not knowing when the bladder is full?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): The move has rather thrown our routine, and the bathroom is still—
[SEG0020] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sorry, he's wandering off. The downstairs loo isn't even plumbed in yet.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Forgive me, doctor. No, my bladder is quite all right. No leaking, and no difficulty passing water.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever, or waking hot and shivery?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): No, doctor. I haven't had a temperature.
[SEG0024] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): That's not quite fair. On Tuesday night you were sweating through the sheets and you felt burning hot. I nearly fetched the thermometer.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): With respect, that was the heating in the new house. It was far too high. I was not ill.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll note that the two of you don't agree about that night, and we can't settle it from here. What about weight — have you lost any?

[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): That's rather difficult, doctor. Since the move we have been living on sandwiches and packet soup, and my trousers feel a little looser. I wouldn't say I have wasted away.
[SEG0028] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His work shirts hang off him. It's more than a little, doctor.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Without trying, and can you put any number on it? Half a stone, a stone?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): I honestly couldn't put a figure on it. I haven't used the scales properly in years. I imagine it is the poor meals, nothing dramatic.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any weakness, legs giving way, or pain shooting below the knee?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No weakness, doctor. The legs are strong, and I can still manage the warehouse stairs. It does not shoot below the knee.
[SEG0033] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): You told me yesterday it shot down to your knee when you twisted.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): That was a single moment, and it settled within the hour. It is not doing that now. I do apologise for the muddle.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not at all, that helps. What are you taking for the pain at the moment?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetamol, by mouth, a thousand milligrams four times a day. I do try, though I often miss the afternoon dose when I am on shift. It takes the edge off, nothing more.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything else — an anti-inflammatory, or something stronger?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): I was taking ibuprofen by mouth, four hundred milligrams three times a day, but I stopped it a fortnight ago. It was upsetting my stomach.
[SEG0039] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): They gave him tramadol at the walk-in centre as well.

[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. Fifty milligrams. I only took the one tablet, felt awfully sick, and stopped. They also offered me diazepam, but I never took that. I don't care for that sort of medicine.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines, or other reactions I ought to know about?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): No, doctor. None that I know of.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any back trouble before this, or any operations?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): No previous back trouble, and I have never had an operation. I am generally well. I don't smoke, and I barely drink.
[SEG0045] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He works in the warehouse at Pendleton's, on his feet all day, lifting. We've just moved to a house with stairs, which is no help at all.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): That is correct, doctor. I am a warehouse operative. The stairs at home are a little trying just now.

[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me examine you, if you'd stand. Forward bending is limited, and you only reach about your knees. Bending backwards is all right. You're tender in the muscles to the right of the lower spine, not on the bone itself.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Straight leg raise is free on both sides, with no pain shooting down. Power and feeling in the feet are normal. Do sit back down.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you. It does catch when I bend, as you saw.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thinking it through, this is simple mechanical low back pain, a muscle strain from the move rather than a trapped nerve. The examination is reassuring on that.

[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): My first thought was an X-ray of the lumbar spine, and naproxen two hundred and fifty milligrams twice a day. An X-ray won't change what we do, though, and naproxen is the same family as the ibuprofen that upset your stomach, so I won't do either of those.

[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): What I will do is refer you to physiotherapy. Keep moving, short walks, no long stretches in bed, and go carefully with lifting until they see you. Carry on with the paracetamol, and don't go back to the anti-inflammatories.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand, doctor. Ought I to worry about that hot night my wife mentioned?

[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): I can't tidy that up without a temperature having been taken. If you get true fevers, or your bladder changes, or you go numb round the saddle area, or a leg becomes weak, you come straight back, or to A&E if we're shut. Don't sit on it.
[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): If it has not settled in six weeks, come back and I might then arrange an MRI of the lower back. If the physio is sorting it, you needn't book in.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): That is very clear. Thank you, doctor. We shall do as you advise.
[SEG0057] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll keep him off the furniture shifting. We're grateful.
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): The referral will go off today. Ask at reception on the way out if you want a nudge about the physio booking. Mind how you go.

spec.situation: Manual worker or office worker with low back pain for 'a few weeks or since the move'; doctor asks about red flags (numbness, bladder, weight loss, fever) one by one; patient answers some clearly, some vaguely or with a story. Painkiller use mentioned.
features: stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.
interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.

bad.reason: Resolved shooting pain lasted within an hour, but 'yesterday' was reported by family, not patient.
bad.text: shooting pain to the knee (category=musculoskeletal, status=resolved, duration=within 1 hour, onset=yesterday on twisting, temporality=resolved, body_site=knee, reported_by=patient, certainty=certain)

bad.reason: Doctor says come back in six weeks if not settled, but responsible person isn't explicitly doctor.
bad.text: Follow-up consultation (action_type=follow_up, status=conditional, responsible_person=doctor, time_reference=value: if it has not settled in six weeks)

omissions.text: Low back pain is more on the right side and is described as a dull ache that becomes quite sharp when bending to lift something.
Pain does not travel into the leg; it stays in the lower back and right buttock.
No pain shooting below the knee currently; the single episode only went down to the knee and settled within an hour.

No fever was reported by the patient; the recorded fact lists fever as present, but the doctor's note was that there was disagreement with the family member about one hot/sweaty night and this could not be settled.

Possible unintentional weight loss was discussed: patient said trousers feel looser and family member said his work shirts hang off him; patient could not quantify any amount and attributed it to poor meals since the move.
Paracetamol 1000 mg four times daily is often not taken as prescribed because he frequently misses the afternoon dose while on shift.
Ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily was stopped a fortnight ago because it upset his stomach.
Tramadol 50 mg caused marked nausea after one tablet and was stopped.
Diazepam was offered by the walk-in centre but he never took it.
Patient is generally well.

Doctor initially considered lumbar spine X-ray and naproxen 250 mg twice a day, but decided against both: X-ray would not change management and naproxen was avoided because it is in the same family as ibuprofen that upset his stomach.
If physiotherapy is helping, he does not need to book follow-up.
Physiotherapy referral will be sent today, and reception can be asked about the physio booking.
